name: Scenario Practice
desc: Production scenarios and exam-trap drills across all five domains — the 'best decision' items that decide pass or fail

questions.q: A team wires a nightly security scan into GitHub Actions with the step: claude "scan the codebase for hardcoded secrets". The job hangs until the workflow timeout fires, then fails with no output. What's wrong?
options: The API key is resolved lazily, so the CLI blocks on an interactive credential prompt that the runner has no way to display
The ANTHROPIC_API_KEY secret is scoped to the repo but not exposed to the job, so the CLI silently retries auth until the timeout
The command omits the -p flag, so Claude Code starts an interactive session and waits on input from a terminal the runner never attaches
Scan-style prompts need an explicit --output-format json, and without it the CLI buffers the whole transcript and never flushes it
questions.explain: Without -p (--print), Claude Code opens an interactive session and waits for input on a terminal that a CI runner never attaches, so it hangs to the workflow timeout. The tempting near-miss is the lazy interactive credential prompt: missing or unexposed credentials produce a fast authentication error and a non-zero exit, not a silent hang for the full timeout window.

questions.q: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code to generate code, then in the SAME session asks it to review that code for bugs. Reviews consistently miss obvious issues. What's the architectural flaw?
options: Temperature sits at its default, so the reviewer samples too conservatively and simply restates the generator's own stated conclusions
Generator and reviewer share one session, so the reviewer is biased toward confirming work already in its context; isolate the reviewer
The generated diff fell into the middle of a very long context, so the reviewer attends to it less reliably than to the ends
The review request follows the generation output, so the earlier reasoning is served from cache and replayed instead of being re-derived
questions.explain: An agent reviewing its own output in the same session treats that output as established context and confirms it; isolating the reviewer as an independent session makes it evaluate the code fresh. The 'lost in the middle' answer is tempting because context length does degrade recall, but the failure here is consistent across every run and every PR size, which points at bias, not position.

questions.q: You want an overnight technical-debt report across the whole repo (not time-sensitive), and separately a blocking pre-merge check that must return fast. Which API choice for each?
options: Use the Message Batches API for both jobs, since batching halves cost and the pre-merge check can poll until results land
Use real-time Messages API calls for both jobs, since a repo-wide sweep can be split into many parallel requests that finish quickly
Use the Message Batches API for the pre-merge gate to smooth rate limits, and real-time calls for the overnight repo-wide report
Use the Message Batches API for the overnight debt report to get the cost discount, and real-time Messages calls for the pre-merge check
questions.explain: Batch processing is the right fit for high-volume work that is not latency-sensitive, so the overnight report belongs there, while a blocking pre-merge gate needs an immediate response and must use real-time requests. Polling a batch for the pre-merge check is the tempting near-miss: the cost math is real, but batch results are not guaranteed to return quickly enough to gate a merge.

questions.q: An automated PR review posts many false-positive comments, annoying developers. Which approach best reduces false positives?
options: Instruct Claude in the system prompt to be careful, flag only genuine issues, and stay silent whenever it is not fully confident
Define explicit categorical review criteria with severity levels, and feed prior findings back into the prompt so duplicates are suppressed
Set temperature to 0 so the reviewer is deterministic and stops emitting speculative comments that vary across repeated runs
Cap the reviewer at the five largest changed files in each PR so it has room to reason carefully and thoroughly about each one
questions.explain: False positives drop when 'issue' is defined categorically with severities the reviewer must map to, and when previous findings are supplied so it stops re-reporting them. Temperature 0 is the tempting near-miss, and it fails twice over: the API docs state that even at temperature 0 results are not fully deterministic, and even if they were, a confidently wrong criterion would just be applied consistently.

questions.q: A coordinator agent delegates research to subagents. Follow-up summarization queries take 40+ seconds because the coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent each time, passing 80,000 tokens of findings it ALREADY holds in its own context. Best fix?
options: Answer the summarization request directly in the coordinator, using the findings already present in its own context
Raise the synthesis subagent's context budget so the 80,000 tokens of findings fit without triggering internal chunking
Compress the findings with a summarization pass before handing them to the synthesis subagent to cut the transfer size
Cache the synthesis subagent's responses so repeat follow-ups on the same findings are served without another spawn
questions.explain: The coordinator already holds the findings, so the summarization needs no delegation at all; doing it inline removes both the spawn overhead and the redundant token transfer. Compressing before the handoff is the tempting near-miss because it shrinks the payload, but it still pays for a spawn and still re-sends data that never had to leave the coordinator.

questions.q: A Claude Agent SDK multi-agent research pipeline crashes after processing 12 of 18 documents, each subagent partially done. Which design best handles this class of failure?
options: Restart the pipeline from the first document on each failure so every subagent runs against one consistent snapshot of state
Raise the per-subagent timeout and add exponential-backoff retries around each document so transient failures stop killing the run
Persist per-document checkpoints so finished work survives the crash and only the unfinished documents are resumed
Collapse all eighteen documents into one long-running agent so there is no cross-agent coordination left to fail
questions.explain: Durable per-document checkpointing is what makes the crash cheap: completed work is preserved and the run resumes only the six unfinished documents. Longer timeouts with backoff retries is the tempting near-miss, but it only addresses transient slowness and still discards the twelve finished documents when the process dies mid-run.

questions.q: When a subagent fails to complete its task in a multi-agent system, what should it return to the coordinator?
options: Return nothing and let the coordinator infer the gap from the missing entry, keeping the failure out of its context window
Return the raw stack trace and full tool transcript so the coordinator has complete fidelity on what went wrong internally
Return a structured error naming what was attempted, the error type, and whether it was an access failure or a genuinely empty result
Return a best-effort partial answer with a low confidence score, so downstream synthesis can weight it instead of branching
questions.explain: The coordinator can only route around a failure if it knows what was tried and whether the source was unreachable or simply held no data, which is exactly what a structured error carries. The best-effort partial with a confidence score is the tempting near-miss: it keeps the pipeline flowing but launders a failure into a claim, so the coordinator cannot tell a lookup error from a real absence.

questions.q: How much context should a coordinator pass to each specialized subagent?
options: Pass only the scoped slice of context each subagent actually needs for its specific task, and nothing beyond that
Give all subagents a shared, append-only context window so their intermediate findings stay mutually visible during the run
Pass just the task instruction and let each subagent rediscover any background it needs through its own tool calls
Pass the full accumulated context to every subagent so each one can reason about how its piece fits the overall task
questions.explain: Each subagent should receive only the narrowly scoped context its task requires, which keeps focus high and token cost low. Passing only the bare instruction and letting subagents rediscover background is the tempting near-miss: it is admirably lean, but it forces redundant tool calls and re-derivation of context the coordinator could simply have handed over.

questions.q: An extraction system must always return customer name, account number, and a cancellation date that may not exist, all as valid JSON. Best approach?
options: Ask in the prompt for clean JSON only with no surrounding prose, and spell out the exact key names to use in the instruction text
Use tool_use with a JSON schema: name and account number required, and the cancellation date typed nullable so absence is representable
Have the model emit free-form text and recover the three fields afterward with regular expressions tuned to the observed output
Mark all three fields required in the schema and drop records where the cancellation date fails downstream date parsing
questions.explain: A schema-backed tool call enforces the shape, and typing the cancellation date as nullable lets the model represent a genuinely absent date instead of inventing one. Marking all three required and discarding unparseable records is the tempting near-miss: it does yield valid JSON, but it pressures the model to fabricate dates and silently throws away otherwise good extractions.

questions.q: Does using tool_use with a JSON schema guarantee the extracted data is correct?
options: Yes, because schema validation constrains generation at decode time, so both the shape and the field values are guaranteed sound
No, tool_use guarantees only structure such as valid types and shape; semantic correctness must be checked separately with business rules
Yes, provided temperature is set to 0 so the extraction becomes deterministic and repeatable for a given input document
No, and a schema adds nothing useful either, since the model may still return keys and types that fall outside the declared shape
questions.explain: A schema can confirm that attendee_count is an integer; it cannot confirm the source document ever stated a number, so semantic checks like cross-field totals belong in your own validation layer. The decode-time constraint answer is the tempting near-miss: constrained generation really does lock the shape, but shape conformance says nothing about whether the value is supported by the source.

questions.q: A Claude-based invoice extraction pipeline using tool_use with a JSON schema sometimes returns output where line items don't sum to the stated total. Best architectural fix for this semantic error?
options: Capture both a calculated_total and the stated_total, compare them in code, and route any mismatch to human review
Add an instruction to the prompt requiring arithmetic to be double-checked before the tool call is emitted for each invoice
Add a line_item_count field to the schema so short or truncated extractions can be detected before the totals are used
Increase max_tokens so long invoices are never truncated mid-table and every line item reaches the extraction output
questions.explain: Extracting the stated total and an independently computed total lets code assert they agree, which turns an invisible semantic error into a caught, reviewable exception. Raising max_tokens is the tempting near-miss: truncation would indeed break sums, but it would also visibly cut the item array short, whereas here the schema is satisfied and only the arithmetic disagrees.

questions.q: In a validation-retry loop, when JSON schema validation fails, what should the retry request include?
options: Re-send the original prompt and document unchanged, relying on a different sample to land on schema-valid output this time
Send only the validation error and the schema, keeping the retry small so the model focuses purely on fixing the shape
Send the document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error, so the correction targets that exact problem
Send the document plus a stricter restatement of the schema, with the previously failing fields marked required a second time
questions.explain: A useful retry is targeted feedback: the source document, the output that failed, and the precise validator message the model must fix. Sending only the error and schema is the tempting near-miss, since it does name the defect, but without the document the model has to re-guess the underlying values rather than repair the one broken field.

questions.q: A customer support agent must never issue a refund over $500 without human approval. Where should this rule be enforced?
options: State the limit in the system prompt, requiring approval before any refund above five hundred dollars is issued to a customer
Encode it in the refund tool's description text so the constraint is visible to the model every time the tool schema is read
Cover it with few-shot examples that show a large refund being declined and routed to a human approver for sign-off
Enforce it as a programmatic hook or gate in the refund tool's execution path that blocks or escalates any amount above the limit
questions.explain: A code-level gate on the refund tool's execution path enforces the threshold regardless of what the model decides, which is what a hard financial limit requires. The tool-description answer is the tempting near-miss: descriptions do strongly steer tool use and sit closer to the call site than a system prompt, but they remain model-read guidance, not enforcement.

questions.q: You have several extraction tools (one per document type) and want Claude to always use one of them, without you pre-choosing which. Which setting?
options: Use tool_choice auto together with a prompt instruction asking Claude to always select one of the extraction tools provided
Use tool_choice any, which guarantees a tool call while leaving Claude to pick which extraction schema fits the document
Use tool_choice tool with the general-purpose extractor named, so there is always a guaranteed call to fall back on
Leave tool_choice unset and validate afterward that a tool_use block is present, retrying the request when one is absent
questions.explain: tool_choice set to 'any' forces exactly one tool call while leaving the schema selection to Claude, which is the requirement here. Naming a single tool with tool_choice 'tool' is the tempting near-miss: it also guarantees a call, but it makes you pre-choose the document type, which is precisely what you wanted to avoid.

questions.q: For a new engineer navigating an unfamiliar codebase, which combination of Claude Code built-in tools is most appropriate for exploration?
options: Grant Bash access alone so the engineer can drive familiar shell tooling like find, grep, and git log directly in the repo
Use Write and Edit as they go, so notes and small clarifying refactors are captured in the code while understanding is fresh
Route exploration through MCP servers only, so every lookup is mediated by an auditable, explicitly configured integration
Use Read, Grep, and Glob to locate and inspect files by pattern and content without modifying anything in the repository
questions.explain: Exploration is a read and search task, and Read, Grep, and Glob cover locating files by name pattern, searching contents, and inspecting them without any write risk. Bash-only is the tempting near-miss because those shell utilities genuinely can search a repo, but it trades the safe read-only surface for arbitrary command execution and loses the structured file-oriented tools.

questions.q: A long-running Claude agent's answer quality degrades on facts that appeared in the middle of a very large context. This is the 'lost in the middle' effect. Best mitigation?
options: Continue appending the relevant history so the buried facts are restated later in the conversation as it keeps growing
Lower the temperature so retrieval from the middle of the context becomes more consistent across repeated questions
Summarize and restructure the context so critical facts sit near the beginning or end rather than buried, and prune irrelevant bulk
Move the transcript into an external store and retrieve only the passages that match each incoming question by keyword
questions.explain: Attention is least reliable over the middle of a very long context, so the fix is to compress, prune, and reposition the important material where it is attended to. External retrieval is the tempting near-miss and is a sound pattern generally, but keyword retrieval can miss the buried facts entirely and does not address a context that is simply too bloated to attend to.

questions.q: A research coordinator gets conflicting facts from two subagents: Agent A says a company's revenue was $4M, Agent B says $6M. Both cite sources. What's the best design principle for resolving this?
options: Preserve provenance for every claim so the coordinator or a human can resolve conflicts by weighing source reliability
Average the two figures to five million dollars so the coordinator has a single value with bounded error either way
Discard both figures and re-run the research pipeline with a narrower revenue prompt until the subagents agree
Accept whichever figure the more recent subagent returned, on the assumption its sources were fetched later and are fresher
questions.explain: Keeping each claim tied to its source is what makes the conflict resolvable, since one figure may be an audited filing and the other a press estimate. Re-running with a narrower prompt is the tempting near-miss: it might produce agreement, but agreement without provenance is not verification, and the disagreement itself is the signal worth keeping.

questions.q: A document genuinely does not contain a shipping date, but your extraction schema marks shipping_date as required. Claude keeps inventing plausible dates. Best fix?
options: Add a few-shot example showing a conservative inference for the shipping date when the document does not state one outright
Make shipping_date nullable in the schema so 'not present' is a representable outcome the model can return honestly
Raise max_tokens so the model has room to scan the full document before it commits to a value for the shipping date
Set temperature to 0 so the model stops sampling speculative dates and returns the same value on every extraction attempt
questions.explain: When the information is genuinely absent, a required field leaves the model no valid way to answer, so it fabricates; making the field nullable gives absence a legitimate representation. Temperature 0 is the tempting near-miss: it does suppress sampling variance, but it makes the invented date consistent rather than making it go away.

questions.q: A CI job runs claude -p with a review prompt, exits with code 0, but the review output is empty/irrelevant (a pattern affecting a meaningful fraction of runs). It's for an authentication module. What's the honest architectural stance?
options: Remove the review step from the pipeline, since an intermittently empty result is worse than having no automated gate there at all
Trust the exit status, since a zero exit from claude -p means the review ran to completion and reported no blocking findings at all
Re-run the review step until it returns non-empty output, then merge on the strength of that one successful run's reported findings
Treat headless review as a first automated check, not final approval: gate auth and payment changes on human review and assert output is on-topic
questions.explain: A zero exit only means the process ran, so the pipeline must assert the output is substantive and relevant, and sensitive modules like authentication still need human approval. Retrying until output appears is the tempting near-miss: it patches the empty-output symptom, but it neither confirms the content is on-topic nor supplies the human sign-off an auth change warrants.

questions.q: Your team wants a critical compliance rule enforced for every Claude Code session, no exceptions, across all developers. Two options seem viable: a strongly-worded CLAUDE.md rule, or a hook. Which, and why is the other a trap?
options: Use CLAUDE.md, since it is loaded into every session automatically and therefore reaches every developer's context reliably
Use CLAUDE.md with the rule restated in a custom slash command, so the constraint is reinjected each time the workflow is invoked
Use CLAUDE.md checked in at the repository root plus a pre-commit lint that greps for the rule text in each developer's checkout
Use a hook, because it enforces the rule as deterministic code; CLAUDE.md is guidance the model can probabilistically fail to follow
questions.explain: A hook runs as code on a defined lifecycle event, so a no-exception compliance rule is enforced regardless of what the model chooses to do. The CLAUDE.md plus pre-commit lint option is the tempting near-miss: it does add a deterministic check, but the lint only verifies the instruction text exists, not that any session actually complied with it.

questions.q: You're architecting on the Claude Agent SDK and deciding between a single Claude agent with tools vs. a multi-agent orchestrator-worker system for a moderately complex task. Which principle should drive the choice?
options: Default to orchestrator-worker because separate workers keep each context window small, which reliably raises answer quality.
Prefer the simplest architecture that meets the need; add multi-agent only when parallelism or isolated specialist contexts genuinely help.
Choose by token budget: a single agent with many tools always costs less than workers, so cost modelling should settle it.
Pick multi-agent whenever the task needs more than one tool, since one agent cannot reliably sequence heterogeneous tools.
questions.explain: Simplicity is the default: orchestration is justified only by real parallelism or context-isolation needs, otherwise it adds cost, latency and new failure modes. The tempting near-miss is the claim that workers keep contexts small and so always improve quality — context isolation only pays off when subtasks are genuinely independent, and this task is merely moderately complex, so coordination overhead dominates.

questions.q: For a production pipeline feeding a database, a teammate proposes prompting Claude to 'respond only with JSON' and parsing the text. Why is this the technically-possible-but-wrong-for-production answer?
options: The failure is the parser: wrapping json.loads in a retry that re-prompts on any error makes prompt-only JSON production-safe.
Prose framing is the problem; asking for JSON inside a fenced code block makes the response schema-conformant by construction.
Text JSON loses type fidelity because the API returns every value as a string, so numeric database columns cannot be inserted.
Prompt-only JSON is fine for prototypes, but pipelines feeding a database need schema-backed structured output or strict tool use.
questions.explain: Prompt-only JSON can drift in shape, so pipelines feeding downstream systems need schema-backed output for reliability and auditability. The tempting near-miss is retrying on parse errors: that catches malformed JSON but not syntactically valid JSON with renamed, missing or extra fields, which is exactly what silently corrupts a database load.

questions.q: A Claude Code generator session in CI produces a 14-file PR. You want Claude to review it thoroughly. What's the best review architecture, and what's the tempting wrong answer?
options: Feed all 14 files into one review pass inside the generator's session so the reviewer keeps full authorial intent and diff context.
Review only the files the generator flagged as risky, then have it re-read its own diff summary to confirm the rest are safe.
Split into per-file review passes plus a final integration pass, run in a reviewer session isolated from the generator.
Run one review pass per file but reuse the generator session, clearing history between files to keep each pass focused.
questions.explain: Per-file passes plus an integration pass, in a session isolated from the generator, avoids both attention loss over a large diff and self-review bias. The tempting near-miss is the single all-14-files pass in the generating session for 'full context' — it is exactly the setup that buries mid-diff issues and lets the author's own rationalisations stand unchallenged.

questions.q: Two MCP tools are named 'search_records' and 'find_records' with near-identical descriptions. Claude frequently calls the wrong one. Best fix?
options: Add a system-prompt decision table mapping query shapes to search_records versus find_records for every case the agent sees.
Rename them search_records_v1 and search_records_v2 so the model can separate them by suffix while descriptions stay as they are.
Leave both tools and set tool_choice to 'any' so the model must commit to a tool call rather than hesitating between names.
Rewrite the two descriptions so each states distinctly when it applies, or consolidate them, so routing follows from the schemas.
questions.explain: Misrouting is a tool-definition problem: distinct, precise descriptions (or one consolidated tool) let the model route from the schema itself. The tempting near-miss is the system-prompt decision table — it can help short-term but leaves the ambiguity in the definitions, drifts out of sync with the tools, and breaks for query shapes the table never enumerated.

questions.q: A verbose subagent returns 20,000 tokens of reasoning, but the coordinator only needs the final 3 extracted facts. What's the best practice for the handoff?
options: Pass the full 20,000 tokens but rely on prompt caching so the coordinator pays very little to re-read the reasoning each turn.
Keep the whole transcript and let the coordinator compact its history once the window fills, so nothing is discarded prematurely.
Have the subagent return a distilled structured result — just the required facts in a defined schema — keeping raw reasoning out.
Have the coordinator summarise the subagent output with a second call, then drop the first half of the original reasoning dump.
questions.explain: Handoffs should carry distilled, schema-shaped results so the coordinator's context stays lean and focused on the three facts it needs. The tempting near-miss is keeping everything and leaning on prompt caching: caching lowers cost but the tokens still occupy the window and dilute attention, which is the actual problem here.

questions.q: You need machine-parseable review findings from claude -p so a downstream script can post inline PR comments. Which flags?
options: Use --verbose with text output so each finding's file and line appears in the log, then parse the labelled lines in the script.
Use --output-format json, optionally with a JSON schema, so findings come back structured and can be parsed programmatically.
Use --output-format stream-json on its own; the last emitted chunk is a clean findings object the downstream script can consume.
Pipe plain output through an appended system prompt asking for CSV rows, then split each returned line on commas in the script.
questions.explain: --output-format json (with a schema when you need a guaranteed shape) gives the downstream script structured findings instead of brittle text parsing. The tempting near-miss is stream-json: it is structured, but it is a stream of message events that requires --verbose in print mode and yields no single findings document, so the script cannot just read one final object.

questions.q: A developer's agent sometimes terminates prematurely when Claude returns text alongside a tool call. Their loop checks response.content[0].type == 'text' to decide if the agent is finished. Users report incomplete responses on complex queries. What should the developer change?
options: Inspect the last content block instead of the first, since Claude emits its tool_use block after any narration text in the turn.
Scan the assistant text for completion phrases such as 'I have finished' and end the loop when one of them appears.
Set tool_choice to 'any' so every turn contains a tool call, making a text-typed first block a reliable end-of-work signal.
Check the stop_reason field instead of content type — continue while it is 'tool_use' and terminate when it is 'end_turn'.
questions.explain: stop_reason is the only authoritative loop-control signal, and it stays correct when text and tool_use blocks arrive in the same turn. The tempting near-miss is checking the last block rather than the first: block ordering is not guaranteed, a turn can carry several tool_use blocks, and it still cannot distinguish end_turn from max_tokens, which stop_reason reports directly.

questions.q: In an agentic loop, after Claude requests a tool with stop_reason 'tool_use', you execute it but the agent seems unable to reason about the result on the next iteration. What's the most likely mistake?
options: The tool result was never appended to the conversation as a new user message, so Claude never sees what the tool returned.
The result was appended but its tool_use_id does not match the request block, so Claude cannot bind it to the pending call.
The result was put into the system prompt for the next request instead of following the assistant's tool_use turn in history.
tool_choice was left at 'auto', so the follow-up request lets Claude answer from memory instead of reading the tool output.
questions.explain: Tool results must be appended to the message history as a user-role tool_result block; skip that and the next request contains nothing new for Claude to reason about. The tempting near-miss is a mismatched tool_use_id — that is a real bug, but it fails loudly with a 400 validation error rather than producing a model that simply seems unaware of the result.

questions.q: You're building a coordinator that delegates to subagents via the Task tool, but subagents behave as if they know nothing about the research context the coordinator has. Why?
options: Subagent prompts are truncated to a fixed token budget, so long research context passed in is dropped before the run begins.
Subagents inherit the parent transcript only up to the last compaction, so everything gathered after it is missing from their view.
The coordinator's allowedTools omits Bash, so delegation silently degrades to a fresh top-level session with no research context.
Subagents run with isolated context and do not inherit parent history, so needed findings must be restated in each subagent prompt.
questions.explain: Subagents start with isolated context and never inherit the coordinator's history, so every relevant finding has to be written into the subagent's prompt. The tempting near-miss is partial inheritance up to the last compaction — ruled out because the subagents behave as if they know nothing at all, not as if they are missing only the most recent stretch.

questions.q: An MCP tool returns an empty array after a customer lookup. Claude retries 3 times, then escalates to a human. Analysis shows the customer's account simply does not exist. What's the root cause of this wasted effort?
options: The tool does not distinguish access failures from valid empty results, so the agent treats 'no matches' as a retriable failure.
The lookup already returns a retriable error flag, so retrying was correct and the real defect is an over-eager escalation rule.
The retry policy lacks exponential backoff, so three rapid attempts hit the same stale cache entry and the agent gave up early.
The tool description omits the account-number format, so the agent sent a malformed identifier that matched nothing in the store.
questions.explain: A successful query that found nothing must be structurally distinct from a failure to reach the data source (empty result: not an error, count zero; access failure: error plus retryable), otherwise the agent burns retries and escalates wrongly. The tempting near-miss is a malformed account identifier, which would also yield an empty array — but the analysis established the account genuinely does not exist, so the query itself was well formed.

questions.q: An MCP tool rejects a refund because it exceeds the £500 policy limit. How should this error be structured so the agent responds correctly?
options: errorCategory 'validation' with isRetryable false, returning the £500 limit so the agent can retry with a reduced refund amount.
errorCategory 'business' with isRetryable false, plus a description directing the agent to escalate to a human approver.
isError false with a status of 'declined', letting the agent treat the rejection as an ordinary successful lookup result.
errorCategory 'transient' with isRetryable true and a short backoff, since approval limits may be widened later in the day.
questions.explain: A policy-limit rejection is a business error that no retry can resolve, so it should be non-retryable with a description pointing the agent to escalation. The tempting near-miss labels it a validation error: it correctly marks it non-retryable, but validation implies a malformed request and invites the agent to quietly reissue a smaller refund instead of escalating a policy decision.

questions.q: A Claude agent has 18 MCP tools available and frequently selects the wrong one; a synthesis-focused subagent even attempts web searches. What principle best addresses this?
options: Keep all 18 tools but list them in the system prompt grouped by role, telling each agent which group it is expected to stay inside.
Keep all 18 available everywhere and rely on tool_choice 'auto' plus richer descriptions to narrow selection at request time.
Scope each agent's tool set to what its role needs, roughly four or five tools, so cross-specialisation misuse becomes impossible.
Put the 18 tools behind one dispatcher tool taking an action name, so the model only ever has a single tool to choose from.
questions.explain: Selection reliability falls as the tool count grows, and an agent cannot misuse a tool it was never given, so scoping each role to a handful of tools is the structural fix. The tempting near-miss is grouping all 18 by role in the system prompt — the synthesis subagent still has web search available, so a soft instruction is all that stands between it and the same wrong call.

questions.q: You want a custom /review slash command available to every developer automatically when they clone or pull the repo. Where do you put it?
options: Commit it as .claude/commands/review.md in the project repository, so it ships with every clone and updates on pull.
Put review.md in ~/.claude/commands/ and have each developer symlink it into the repo so one definition serves everyone.
Define the command as a fenced block inside the repo's root CLAUDE.md, which is version-controlled and loaded automatically.
Register it in .claude/settings.json under a commands array that points at the markdown file, so the repo publishes it.
questions.explain: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ are version-controlled, so cloning or pulling the repo gives every developer the command automatically. The tempting near-miss is a user-level file symlinked into the repo — the symlink can be committed but its target lives outside version control, so a fresh clone resolves to nothing on a machine that lacks the home-directory file.

questions.q: Test files are spread throughout the codebase (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx) and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location, applied automatically. Best mechanism?
options: A testing skill holding the conventions in SKILL.md, invoked whenever someone starts work on one of the test files.
A single root CLAUDE.md with a per-area section, relying on Claude to infer which conventions apply to the file being edited.
A CLAUDE.md in every directory containing tests, so the nearest file is picked up as the tree is walked upward from the file.
Path-scoped files in .claude/rules/ with glob frontmatter such as paths ['**/*.test.tsx'], loading whenever a match is edited.
questions.explain: Glob-scoped rule files attach conventions to a filename pattern rather than a directory, so they load for every matching test file wherever it sits. The tempting near-miss is per-directory CLAUDE.md files, which really do load hierarchically — but with tests beside every component you would duplicate that file across the whole tree, and it still applies to all files in the folder rather than to test files specifically.

questions.q: A skill produces very verbose codebase-analysis output that pollutes the main conversation context. Which frontmatter option fixes this?
options: argument-hint — prompting the caller for a narrower target path up front keeps the analysis, and so the output, small.
allowed-tools — restricting the skill to read-only tools keeps it from producing a large analysis dump in the transcript.
context: fork — the skill runs in an isolated subagent context, so its verbose output stays out of the main conversation.
disable-model-invocation — removing automatic triggering means the dump only enters context when a user asks for it.
questions.explain: context: fork executes the skill in an isolated subagent context and returns only its result, so verbose exploration never lands in the main session. The tempting near-miss is disable-model-invocation: it does cut how often the skill fires, but every explicit invocation still dumps the full verbose output into the main conversation, so the pollution is unchanged when the skill is actually used.

questions.q: A new team member reports they're not getting the coding-standard instructions everyone else follows. The rules were placed in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md by another dev. What's the diagnosis?
options: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is not version-controlled, so team-wide standards must sit at project level to reach teammates.
The rules are at project level but excluded by the repo's ignore rules for .claude/, so they never reached the new clone.
The new member's session loaded the rules but hit the CLAUDE.md size limit, so the coding-standards section was truncated.
CLAUDE.md @path imports resolve only on the author's machine, so the standards file referenced from it was never loaded.
questions.explain: A user-level CLAUDE.md applies to that one user's machine and is never distributed, so shared standards belong in the project so they arrive on clone or pull; /memory shows which files loaded. The tempting near-miss blames a gitignored .claude/ directory — ruled out because the stem states the rules were placed in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which was never in the repository at all.

questions.q: An extraction schema marks shipping_date as required, but some source documents genuinely lack a shipping date, and Claude keeps fabricating plausible dates. Best fix?
options: Keep the field required but add a paired shipping_date_confidence value so downstream code can discard low-confidence dates.
Set temperature to 0 so the model deterministically copies the source text instead of sampling a plausible-looking date value.
Make shipping_date nullable or optional so 'not present' is representable and the model need not invent a value to satisfy it.
Switch to strict tool use so schema validation rejects any date that does not literally appear in the source document text.
questions.explain: A required field with no source value pushes the model to fabricate one; making it nullable gives 'absent' a legal representation. The tempting near-miss is a paired confidence score — it still forces a date into the required field, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so fabricated dates keep flowing downstream with respectable-looking scores.

questions.q: Your automated Claude Code review in CI posts many false positives, eroding developer trust. Which approach most effectively improves precision?
options: Have the model score each finding's confidence and suppress everything below a threshold, tightening that bar over time.
Set temperature to 0 so the reviewer stops sampling speculative findings and returns the same set of findings on every run.
Write explicit categorical criteria naming which issues to report and which to skip, with concrete examples per severity level.
Add 'be conservative' and 'report only high-confidence findings' to the review prompt so the model raises its own bar.
questions.explain: Explicit categories with worked examples give the model a consistent classification boundary, which is what actually raises precision; you can also mute a noisy category while you refine it. The tempting near-miss is threshold-filtering self-rated confidence — model confidence is poorly calibrated, so it hides genuine bugs while confidently-worded false positives sail through.

questions.q: In your research system the coordinator keeps passing web-search payloads to analyze_document instead of analyze_content. Both descriptions read "analyzes content and returns findings". What fixes the misrouting?
options: Add a system prompt rule routing web results to analyze_content and documents to analyze_document, overriding both descriptions
Force analyze_content with tool_choice on any coordinator turn that immediately follows a web search step in the pipeline
Attach input_examples of web-search payloads to analyze_content so the coordinator can pattern-match on the shape of its input
Rename each tool and rewrite its description to state its purpose, expected input, and when to use it rather than the other one
questions.explain: Tool descriptions are the primary signal Claude uses to select a tool, so near-identical wording is the actual defect; renaming and differentiating them by purpose, input format, and boundary resolves it at the source. The system prompt rule is the tempting near-miss: it can steer selection, but it leaves the ambiguous descriptions in place, so the misrouting returns wherever the rule does not explicitly reach.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent. Claude's answer quality degrades on important details (amounts, dates, order numbers) buried in the middle of a long conversation. What's the best mitigation?
options: Keep transactional facts — amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses — in a persistent case-facts block placed at the prompt edges.
Reverse the message order each turn so the oldest turns sit last, moving buried details into the recency window instead.
Enable prompt caching on the conversation prefix so earlier turns are re-read verbatim each turn instead of being skimmed.
Progressively summarise older turns into a running recap so the whole history stays short enough to be attended to reliably.
questions.explain: Because attention is weakest in the middle of long inputs, pinning exact transactional values into a structured facts block near the start or end keeps them reliably available. The tempting near-miss is progressive summarisation: it does shorten history, but summaries paraphrase and blur precise amounts, dates and order numbers — exactly the details the agent is getting wrong.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Multi-Agent Research System. While Claude synthesises findings from multiple sources, two credible sources report conflicting revenue figures ($4M vs $6M). How should the synthesis handle this?
options: Reconcile to a single $5M midpoint and footnote that the underlying sources disagreed on the exact revenue total
Report both figures with the source attached to each rather than picking one, keeping claim-to-source mappings intact for the reader
Prefer the higher figure and note that the lower source is likely reporting a pre-adjustment or net-of-returns number
Withhold both figures and report only the qualitative findings the two sources agree on, flagging revenue as unresolved
questions.explain: Conflicting values from credible sources should be surfaced with their attribution so the reader or coordinator can adjudicate using dates and methodology. The tempting answer is the footnoted midpoint, but averaging invents a figure no source reported and destroys the claim-source mapping the scenario depends on.

questions.q: During a long codebase-exploration session, the agent starts giving inconsistent answers and referencing 'typical patterns' instead of the specific classes it found earlier. Best countermeasure?
options: Continue the session; later turns re-ground themselves on the earlier tool results once a class name comes up again
Record key findings in a scratchpad file the agent re-reads for later questions, and /compact once discovery output fills context
Raise max_tokens so each answer has room to restate the specific classes that were discovered earlier in the session
Re-read every relevant source file at the start of each question so the discovery output is always freshly in context
questions.explain: Drift toward generic 'typical patterns' is context degradation: the specific findings have aged out or been buried. A scratchpad plus /compact persists conclusions across context boundaries. Re-reading every file each question is tempting and does re-ground the model, but it re-floods the same context that is already overfull, so the degradation returns immediately.

questions.q: An unattended Agent SDK job in production occasionally runs for hours and burns a large bill before anyone notices. Which combination best bounds it?
options: Wrap the run in an external wall-clock timeout that kills the process, and inspect the logs afterwards to see what it spent
Set max_turns and max_budget_usd as hard termination ceilings, and read total_cost_usd from each ResultMessage for cost observability
Lower temperature and trim the system prompt so each turn carries fewer tokens and the loop converges on the task sooner
Restrict the allowed tool set so the agent has fewer actions available and therefore fewer opportunities to keep looping
questions.explain: Unattended loops need explicit in-loop ceilings (max_turns, max_budget_usd) plus cost telemetry from ResultMessage. The external wall-clock kill is the strong near-miss: it does bound runtime, but it bounds only time, not spend, and it terminates mid-task with no cost figure, so nobody learns what the run cost.

questions.q: A long orchestrator session gets progressively more expensive per turn even though individual tasks stay the same size. What explains this, and what's the mitigation?
options: Output tokens are priced above input tokens, so an orchestrator that narrates each delegation pays a rising premium as its own responses lengthen
Prompt caching expires between turns in a long session, so previously cached history is re-billed at full input rates each time the cache window lapses
Each subagent result is appended to the orchestrator transcript twice, once as a tool result and once as a summary, doubling the tokens carried forward
Every call re-sends the full history plus all subagent descriptions, so per-turn cost grows with session length; cap turns, use cheaper subagent models, reset sessions
questions.explain: Cost climbs because the orchestrator re-sends accumulated history and all subagent descriptions on every call, so mitigation is turn caps, cheaper subagent models, and session resets. Cache expiry is the tempting answer, but a lapsed cache would produce a spike and reset, not the steady per-turn growth described in the scenario.

questions.q: SCENARIO - Multi-Agent Research System. A long coordinator-driven analysis pipeline was interrupted partway through. The next run must pick up where it stopped instead of repeating work that already finished. How do you design for this?
options: Have each subagent append findings into the final report file, then rebuild the pipeline's state by parsing that report back
Have the coordinator hold each subagent's returned summary in its own context, so a restart can replay those summaries from it
Have the coordinator re-dispatch every subagent and let each one work out from its own prior output that the work was done
Have each subagent persist its completed findings and a status marker to a shared state file the coordinator reads on restart
questions.explain: Durable resumption needs state written outside any agent's context: a shared file recording per-subtask findings and completion status lets the coordinator restart and skip finished work. The near-miss is keeping summaries in the coordinator's context, which is exactly the thing an interruption or a compaction destroys.

questions.q: SCENARIO - Multi-Agent Research System. A discovery subagent must read widely across the repository during a planning phase, and you need a guarantee that it cannot modify anything while it explores. How do you configure it?
options: Give the coordinator the write tools and have the subagent request each edit through it once the discovery pass has finished
Give the subagent the full tool set but a system prompt instructing it never to write or edit files during the discovery pass
Run the subagent first and review its transcript for writes before letting the coordinator act on anything it has reported
Give the subagent a tool set restricted to read-only tools, plus a system prompt constraining its role to reporting findings
questions.explain: A guarantee comes from the tool allowlist: if write tools are not granted, the subagent cannot write, and the role-constraining prompt keeps its output on task. The near-miss grants everything and forbids writing in the prompt, which is instruction rather than enforcement and fails exactly when the model misreads the task.

questions.q: SCENARIO - Developer Productivity with Claude. A lead wants every clone of the repo to pick up the same coding standards automatically, while each engineer keeps personal preferences that nobody else should inherit. How should this be split?
options: Commit the shared standards as project-level configuration, and keep personal preferences in each engineer's user-level config
Commit the shared standards as project-level configuration, and have engineers add personal preferences under their own headings
Keep everything in each engineer's user-level configuration, and circulate a copy of that file to the team whenever it changes
Keep the standards on a wiki page and ask engineers to paste the relevant section into their prompt at the start of a session
questions.explain: Project-level configuration is committed and therefore shared on clone, while user-level configuration is per-machine and never travels through version control, which is precisely the split the lead wants. The near-miss keeps the project file but folds personal preferences into it, so one engineer's preferences get committed and imposed on everyone.

questions.q: SCENARIO - Claude Code for Continuous Integration. CLAUDE.md tells Claude to run the test suite before it reports a task finished. It usually does, but under long sessions it sometimes skips it. You need this to happen every time.
options: Add the instruction to each engineer's user-level memory, so it applies in every repository where they run Claude Code locally
Repeat the instruction in the session prompt as well as CLAUDE.md, so the requirement stays close to the model at decision time
Move the instruction into a Skill, so the model loads a detailed testing procedure whenever the task looks test related to it
Configure a hook so the suite runs automatically as part of the workflow, rather than depending on the model deciding to run it
questions.explain: When a step must happen deterministically, it belongs in a hook, because hooks execute as part of the workflow instead of relying on the model to choose the action. The near-miss reinforces the same instruction in the prompt: it improves the odds but leaves the step discretionary, which is the failure already being observed.

questions.q: A developer runs `claude` from /tmp while working on a repo elsewhere and reports that none of the project's MCP servers or project settings load. What's the cause?
options: Project-scope configuration resolves relative to the working directory, so Claude Code must be launched from the repo root or a subdirectory to load it
Project-scoped MCP servers require per-project approval, and an unapproved .mcp.json is skipped silently along with the rest of the project config
Additional directories added at runtime supply file access but not configuration, so the repo's servers load only after it is trusted as the primary root
Project settings merge in only at the first tool call, so a session started elsewhere keeps user-scope configuration for its whole lifetime
questions.explain: Project-scope discovery is directory-based: launched from /tmp, the repo's .mcp.json and .claude/settings.json are never found. The approval-prompt answer is tempting since unapproved .mcp.json servers really are skipped, but that would not also drop project settings, and the developer reports both are missing.

questions.q: You want to trial a new hook on your own machine before proposing it to the team, without affecting teammates or committing anything. Where does it go?
options: .claude/settings.json in the repo, since a hook needs project context and can be reverted before anyone pulls the change
.claude/settings.local.json, which is scoped to this repo, outranks project settings, and is gitignored so teammates are unaffected
~/.claude/settings.json, which keeps it off the repo entirely while you evaluate it across your own day-to-day work
managed-settings.json, so the hook is applied consistently and can be withdrawn centrally once the trial is finished
questions.explain: settings.local.json is the experimentation layer: repo-scoped, higher precedence than project settings, and automatically gitignored. User-level settings.json is the tempting near-miss since it also avoids a commit, but it applies the untested hook to every project you touch instead of just this repo.

questions.q: A programmatic consumer needs machine-readable results from an Agent SDK run, not prose. What's the correct mechanism?
options: Instruct the model to end with a fenced JSON block and extract it from the assistant text with a regex in the consumer
Define a tool whose input schema is the result shape and treat the model's final tool_use input as the machine-readable payload
Pass a JSON Schema as outputFormat and read the parsed result from the structured_output field on the result message
Set temperature to 0 and pin the model version so the prose layout stays stable enough for a fixed field parser
questions.explain: The SDK takes a JSON Schema via outputFormat and exposes the parsed object as structured_output, which is the supported path. The tool-schema trick is a genuinely used pattern and tempting, but it constrains a tool call rather than the run's result, so the consumer still has to dig the payload out of the transcript.

questions.q: A Claude extraction pipeline validates every tool_use response against its JSON Schema and all responses pass, yet downstream reports contain wrong figures. What kind of validation is missing?
options: Stricter schema constraints: add enums, numeric minimums and maximums, and required fields so out-of-range values are rejected before they reach the report
Response-level validation: verify the stop reason was tool_use and that no max_tokens truncation occurred, since a cut-off call can still parse as valid JSON
Semantic validation: the schema proves shape and types, not that the source supports the values, so add business-rule and provenance checks and route mismatches to review
Input validation: confirm each source document was fully extracted and legible first, so the model is never asked to read a partial or skewed page
questions.explain: Schema validation guarantees structure, not truth: it cannot confirm the document said the number or that line items sum to the total, so business-rule and provenance checks are required. Tighter schema constraints are the tempting answer, but range and enum rules are still shape checks and pass cleanly on a confidently wrong figure.

questions.q: You must extract from exactly one known document type and want to eliminate any chance the model picks a different tool or replies conversationally. Which tool_choice setting?
options: Force the specific tool with {type: 'tool', name: 'extract_invoice'}, removing both the text-response path and the tool-selection decision
Use tool_choice: 'any' so a tool call is mandatory, relying on there being only one tool defined to make the selection unambiguous
Use tool_choice: 'auto' with a prompt that states the tool must always be called and that prose replies are unacceptable
Use tool_choice: 'none' and put the schema in the prompt, then validate the returned JSON text against that schema in the consumer
questions.explain: With one known document type, naming the tool eliminates conversational replies and wrong-tool selection together. tool_choice 'any' is the strong near-miss: it does forbid text, but it leaves selection to the model, which matters as soon as a second tool is added and is not the guarantee the scenario asks for.

questions.q: A Claude reviewer agent's findings vary run to run on identical input — sometimes flagging a pattern, sometimes not. Which change most improves consistency?
options: Set temperature to 0 so sampling stops varying between runs and identical input yields the same set of review findings every time
Replace subjective instructions with explicit categorical criteria and severity definitions, each illustrated with concrete examples
Run the review three times and report only findings appearing in at least two runs, treating single-run hits as sampling noise
Raise max_tokens so the reviewer is never truncated mid-analysis and always reaches the later sections of the diff under review
questions.explain: Run-to-run variation on identical input usually reflects underspecified criteria, so explicit categories and severity definitions with worked examples give the model a repeatable rubric. Temperature 0 is the tempting fix and does reduce sampling variance, but it makes an ambiguous rubric consistently applied rather than correctly applied, so borderline patterns stay mis-scored.

questions.q: After connecting a database MCP server, sessions start hitting context limits quickly and Claude warns about oversized tool output. What's the right response?
options: Raise the MCP output token limit so large result sets are returned whole instead of being truncated part-way through a query response
Narrow what the tool returns using specific fields, row limits and pagination, since a chatty server burns the context the task needs
Move the database server to user scope so its tool definitions and results load lazily rather than with every single project session
Wrap the queries so results are written to a file and only the file path is returned, keeping the full result set available on disk
questions.explain: MCP tool output is warned about near 10,000 tokens and hard-capped by default, so the fix belongs on the tool side: scoped fields, row limits and pagination. Raising the cap is tempting and removes the warning, but it just moves more tokens into the same finite context window and worsens the limit problem described.

questions.q: A team's .mcp.json is committed to a public repo and includes an Authorization header for a remote server. What's the correct remediation?
options: Rewrite git history to purge the header from every commit, then keep the same .mcp.json so the team's shared config stays intact
Replace the inline header with a reference to a .env file listed in .gitignore, so the value is no longer stored in .mcp.json itself
Rotate the leaked credential first, then use environment-variable expansion in .mcp.json, or move that server to local or user scope
Switch the server from remote http to stdio behind a local wrapper that reads the token from the OS keychain at process start
questions.explain: The credential is already public, so rotation comes first, then env-var expansion in .mcp.json or moving the server to local/user scope keeps secrets out of the commit. History rewriting is the tempting near-miss, but it does not invalidate a key that clones, forks and caches may already hold.

questions.q: SCENARIO - Structured Data Extraction. In a long Agent SDK run, summarisation of older turns has blurred the normalisation conventions the agent had been following, and extraction output has started to drift. What is the durable fix?
options: Keep the conventions in a compact structured state object that is re-injected on every turn, outside whatever gets summarised
Have the agent restate the conventions in each of its own replies, so the most recent turns always carry them forward intact
Raise the threshold at which the session summarises, so older turns survive considerably longer before they are condensed away
Split the run into shorter sessions and let each one rediscover the conventions from the documents that it happens to process
questions.explain: Critical instructions should be held in a small structured state block that is selectively retained and re-injected, so summarisation of the conversation cannot erode them. The near-miss has the agent restate conventions each turn: it survives a sliding window, but the restatement is itself model output that drifts and is eventually summarised too.

questions.q: A coordinator must decide what a research subagent returns. The subagent produced 25,000 tokens of exploration to reach four conclusions. What should cross the boundary?
options: A model-written prose summary of the reasoning path alongside the four conclusions, so the coordinator can see how each one was reached
The four conclusions plus the tool results that produced them, so the coordinator can re-verify each claim without resuming the subagent
Only a distilled structured result: the four conclusions in a defined schema with source attribution, since the raw transcript persists separately for audit
The first several thousand tokens of exploration followed by the conclusions, keeping the early framing that shaped the later analysis
questions.explain: Handoffs should carry distilled, schema-shaped results with attribution so the coordinator's context stays lean; the audit trail survives because subagent transcripts persist and can be resumed via agentId. Attaching the supporting tool results is the tempting near-miss, but that re-imports the bulk the boundary exists to keep out, and the 25,000 tokens remain retrievable anyway.

questions.q: A Claude research agent must fetch three independent data sources before it can synthesise. Latency is dominated by round trips. What's the correct architectural response?
options: Have the agentic loop emit multiple tool_use blocks in one response turn so the independent fetches execute in parallel and return together
Spawn three subagents so each fetch runs in its own isolated context, then have the coordinator merge their three transcripts
Raise max_turns so the three sequential fetches have room to complete before the loop hits its turn ceiling and truncates
Collapse the three sources behind one composite tool that fetches all of them, so the model spends only one turn on retrieval
questions.explain: Independent fetches with no data dependency should be issued as multiple tool_use blocks in a single turn so they run in parallel, collapsing three round trips into one. The composite-tool answer is the tempting near-miss — it does cut turns, but the scenario says the three sources are independent and already exist as separate tools, so batching the calls gets the same win without rewriting integrations.

questions.q: Your loop executes tool calls one at a time even when Claude returns several tool_use blocks in a single response. What's the consequence and the fix?
options: You discard parallelism Claude already offered — run that turn's tool_use blocks concurrently and return all tool_result blocks together
Nothing is lost architecturally: the Messages API requires tool_result blocks to be returned one per message, so serial execution is mandatory
Return only the first tool_result and let Claude re-request the rest, so each call is confirmed before the next one is dispatched
Set tool_choice to 'any' so each turn yields exactly one tool_use block and your serial executor matches the model's output shape
questions.explain: Multiple tool_use blocks in one turn mean Claude has already judged those calls independent; executing them concurrently and returning all tool_result blocks in one follow-up message recovers the latency win. The tool_choice='any' option is the near-miss — it does force tool use but does not cap a response at one tool call, and it fixes the symptom by removing the parallelism instead of using it.

questions.q: You're writing delegation instructions for a research subagent. Which approach best balances adaptive behaviour with coordinator visibility?
options: Goal-oriented: state the outcome and success criteria plus a required output schema, so the coordinator keeps visibility as the subagent adapts
Procedural: enumerate the exact tool calls and their order so every run is reproducible and the coordinator can audit each step
Give the topic and the output schema only, omitting success criteria so the subagent stays maximally free to define what 'done' means
Give a procedural script but allow the subagent to skip any step it judges unnecessary, reporting afterwards which steps it dropped
questions.explain: Goal-oriented delegation lets the subagent adapt as it learns, while a required output contract preserves the coordinator's visibility. The tempting near-miss is topic-plus-schema with no success criteria: it keeps the coordinator's visibility but drops the definition of done, so the subagent cannot judge sufficiency — the scenario explicitly asks for balance, not maximal autonomy.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates with the instruction 'search the web, then read the top three results, then summarise'. Subagents frequently return thin findings when the top results are irrelevant. What's the flaw?
options: The subagent's context window fills with search results before it reaches the summarisation step, so its final report is truncated
The coordinator passes no conversation history, so the subagent lacks the background needed to judge which search results are relevant
The delegation is procedural — it prescribes a fixed sequence, so the subagent follows the script even when interim results show it is failing
Web search should be dropped from the subagent's toolset in favour of a curated document store that the coordinator assembles and supplies
questions.explain: A fixed procedural sequence executes regardless of intermediate findings, so a subagent told to read the top three results reads them even when they are irrelevant; a goal-oriented brief with reformulation criteria lets it adapt. The missing-history option is the near-miss — background can help relevance judgements, but the scenario shows the subagent completing all three prescribed steps, which is scripted compliance rather than a knowledge gap.

questions.q: You define a subagent in the Agent SDK, but the coordinator never spawns it — it attempts the work itself instead. Nothing errors. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
options: The subagent's system prompt is too terse for the coordinator's matcher to score it as relevant to the incoming request
Subagent definitions must also be declared in CLAUDE.md before the coordinator will treat them as spawnable at runtime
The subagent's description does not match the task wording, so the coordinator scores it as a poor fit and handles the request itself
The Task/Agent tool is absent from the coordinator's allowedTools, so it has no mechanism to delegate and silently does the work inline
questions.explain: Delegation is explicit wiring: with no Task (Agent) tool in the coordinator's allowed tool list there is no mechanism to spawn anything, so it completes the work inline without erroring. The vague-description option is the strong near-miss — a poor description really can suppress selection, but that usually shows up as inconsistent delegation, whereas here the subagent is never spawned at all.

questions.q: A subagent spawns but immediately fails every task, reporting it cannot access the files it needs. The coordinator works fine. Where do you look first?
options: The coordinator's system prompt, since the delegation brief it passes is what determines the subagent's effective file access
The subagent's AgentDefinition — its tool restrictions most likely omit the read tools (Read/Grep/Glob) that its role requires
The MCP server transport setting, since a stdio server started per session may not expose filesystem resources to child agents
The working directory the subagent inherits, which may resolve the coordinator's relative paths outside the mounted project tree
questions.explain: Subagents receive their own tool access scoped by their definition, so a role that must inspect files needs Read/Grep/Glob granted explicitly; check tool permissions first, then AgentDefinition parameters, then coordinator wiring. The working-directory option is the near-miss — a wrong cwd does produce missing-file errors, but the subagent reports it cannot access files at all and fails every task, not just path-relative ones.

questions.q: A Claude research pipeline is built as a fixed 5-step sequence. When early findings reveal an unexpected subtopic, the pipeline ignores it and produces incomplete coverage. What design change addresses this?
options: Run the same five-step sequence once per candidate subtopic and merge all the outputs, letting sheer breadth substitute for adaptivity
Extend the fixed sequence with extra steps that anticipate the subtopics human reviewers have most often flagged as missing in past runs
Decompose into dynamically generated subtasks that adapt as new information surfaces, rather than a predetermined sequence run regardless of findings
Insert a coverage-check step at the end that flags gaps, then rerun the whole five-step sequence with those gaps appended to the brief
questions.explain: A predetermined sequence cannot respond to what it learns; dynamic decomposition lets the coordinator generate new subtasks from intermediate findings, which is what produces full coverage when the topic's shape is unknown. The end-of-run coverage check is the tempting near-miss — it eventually catches gaps, but only after a full wasted pass, and the scenario's problem is that findings surfacing mid-run are ignored.

questions.q: For a task where the required subtasks genuinely cannot be known before exploration begins, which coordinator design is appropriate?
options: Pre-generate the complete subtask list on the first turn so cost and runtime are predictable before any exploration happens
Run an initial scoping pass, generate subtasks from what it actually finds, and re-evaluate coverage as each result returns
Delegate the whole task to one broadly scoped subagent and let it decide its own subtasks as it explores the problem
Pre-generate a subtask list but attach a confidence score to each, dropping the low-confidence ones once exploration begins
questions.explain: Explore-then-decompose fits: a scoping pass establishes the real shape of the problem, subtasks are generated from actual findings, and coverage is re-evaluated as results arrive. Pre-generating with confidence scores is the near-miss — it looks adaptive, but it can only prune assumptions made before exploration and never adds the subtasks nobody could have predicted.

questions.q: Three independent documents each need the same analysis, and results are combined at the end. Which orchestration pattern fits, and which would be wrong?
options: Nested subagents, each one spawning the next and passing its findings down, so the innermost agent produces the combined result
A sequential pipeline, so that each document's analysis can inform how the next document is approached, weighted, and interpreted
One agent processing all three documents in a single shared context, so cross-document continuity is preserved for the final merge
Parallel execution under a coordinator, since the three analyses are independent; a sequential pipeline serialises work that has no dependencies
questions.explain: Pattern choice follows the dependency graph: independent tasks with a final merge map to coordinator-managed parallel execution. Single-context processing is the tempting near-miss — continuity sounds useful for the merge step, but the scenario states the documents are independent, so one shared context just serialises the work and burns context window.

questions.q: A workflow must extract data, then validate it against the extracted values, then generate a report from the validated data. Which pattern, and why not parallel?
options: A sequential pipeline, since each stage consumes the prior stage's output; parallelising would run validation before the data it validates exists
Coordinator-worker with three independent workers, one per stage, coordinated through a shared results store that they each poll
Parallel execution across the three stages, with each stage retrying on failure until the inputs it depends on eventually become available
A single tool call performing extraction, validation, and reporting internally, so no orchestration layer is needed around it at all
questions.explain: Each stage strictly consumes the previous stage's output, so the stages must run sequentially; parallelism only helps where tasks are genuinely independent. The one-big-tool option is the near-miss — it does preserve the ordering internally, but the question asks which orchestration pattern fits, and hiding all three stages in one call gives up the per-stage validation and visibility the workflow needs.

questions.q: Claude Code generates tests that pass but assert almost nothing meaningful (checking that a function returns 'defined'). How do you raise generation quality?
options: Ask for many more tests per file, so that the trivial assertions are diluted by a much larger share of meaningful behavioural ones
Have Claude generate the assertions first and the test scaffolding second, so assertion quality is decided before setup code exists
Require a branch-coverage threshold in the prompt, so generation continues until every branch of the function under test is exercised
Supply existing test files as context to fix fixture conventions, and state criteria separating meaningful behavioural assertions from trivial ones
questions.explain: Quality comes from concrete context plus explicit criteria: sample tests transfer fixture and naming conventions, and stated criteria define what counts as a meaningful behavioural assertion rather than an existence check. The coverage-threshold option is the strong near-miss — branch coverage does force more code paths to be touched, but a test can execute a branch and still only assert the result is defined, which is exactly the observed failure.

questions.q: Generated tests are behaviourally reasonable but don't compile — they invent fixture helpers and setup patterns your suite doesn't have. Best fix?
options: Post-process the generated tests with a script that rewrites the imports and helper names so they match your suite's real fixtures
Instruct the prompt to use only fixtures that already exist in the repository and to avoid defining any new helper functions
Provide representative existing test files as context so Claude follows your real fixture conventions rather than inventing plausible ones
Point Claude at the test runner's configuration file so that it can infer the available fixtures from the suite's setup entries
questions.explain: The model invents plausible fixtures because it has never seen yours; representative example files are the reliable way to transfer convention. The config-file option is the near-miss — runner config does list setup files and paths, but it does not show helper signatures or usage patterns, which is what the generated tests are getting wrong.

questions.q: A single Claude review prompt asks for security issues, business-logic bugs, and API design feedback at once. Recall on each concern is mediocre. What's the fix?
options: Run specialised review passes separating the concerns, each with its own focused prompt and dedicated few-shot examples, avoiding recall trade-offs
Merge the three concerns into one longer, more emphatic prompt that enumerates each category and demands equal attention to all three
Keep the single prompt but require findings to be emitted grouped by concern, so each category is addressed explicitly before the next
Keep the single pass and raise temperature so the model explores more angles and surfaces findings it would otherwise rank as marginal
questions.explain: Competing concerns in one prompt force recall trade-offs; separate passes with concern-specific examples let each dimension get full attention, at the cost of extra calls. Grouping the output by concern is the tempting near-miss — it improves report structure, but the model is still reasoning about all three concerns in one pass, so recall on each stays mediocre.

questions.q: You've split your Claude Code CI reviews into security, business-logic, and API-design passes. Each pass now needs to reach production quality. What most improves each pass individually?
options: Reuse the same generic few-shot examples across all three passes so that findings stay consistently formatted and comparable
Give each pass dedicated few-shot examples drawn from its own concern, plus explicit inclusion and exclusion boundaries for that category
Raise max_tokens on all three passes so no pass has to truncate its reasoning before reporting every finding it identified
Run each pass twice with different phrasings and take the union of findings, so anything either run surfaced reaches the report
questions.explain: Splitting passes pays off only when each gets concern-specific examples and explicit inclusion/exclusion boundaries, which is what defines the category for that pass. Running each pass twice and unioning is the near-miss — it can add recall, but it doubles cost and amplifies false positives without ever telling a pass what belongs in its category.

questions.q: In a Claude extraction pipeline, dates arrive in mixed forms — '3/4/26', 'March 4 2026', '2026-03-04' — breaking downstream parsing. Schema validation passes each time. Best fix?
options: Add a downstream normaliser that regex-matches every date format you have observed so far and rewrites each one to a canonical form
Put format normalisation in the extraction prompt — always ISO 8601 YYYY-MM-DD — alongside the schema, so output is consistent at source
Set the field's JSON Schema type to string with format 'date', relying on the validator to reject any value that is not ISO 8601
Retype the field as a plain string and defer all interpretation to the consumer, which already knows which locale each source uses
questions.explain: The schema types the field loosely enough that every observed form validates, so the canonical representation has to be specified in the extraction instructions — state ISO 8601 and consistency is produced at source.
