The format:'date' option is the strong near-miss: it names a real JSON Schema annotation, but format is advisory and commonly unenforced, and the scenario already reports validation passing on every variant.

questions.q: A status field should only ever be one of pending, shipped, delivered, cancelled, but Claude sometimes returns 'in transit' or 'on the way'. Which schema change fixes this?
options: Define the field as an enum over the four permitted values, so anything outside that set is structurally invalid rather than merely discouraged
Make the field nullable so that unrecognised statuses can be emitted as null and then filtered out before the value reaches consumers
Add a few-shot example showing each of the four statuses in use, so the model generalises from the demonstrated status vocabulary
Spell out the four allowed values in the field's description text, so the model is told plainly which statuses are acceptable here
questions.explain: An enum constrains the field to a fixed value set at the schema level, making out-of-set values invalid rather than just disfavoured. The few-shot option is the tempting near-miss — examples do steer vocabulary and would reduce 'in transit', but they remain guidance, so an unlisted value still validates; only the enum enforces the closed set.

questions.q: SCENARIO — Customer Support Resolution Agent. A conversation runs long and the full history no longer fits Claude's context. Which retention strategy preserves answer quality best?
options: Pair a sliding window of recent turns with a structured state object holding durable facts (order IDs, amounts, entitlements) plus key decisions
Truncate to just the most recent N messages and discard everything older, keeping the window small enough to stay well under the limit
Summarise the entire conversation into a single paragraph each time the limit approaches, and carry only that paragraph forward afterwards
Keep a sliding window and re-summarise the dropped turns into a rolling prose recap that is prepended to every new request
questions.explain: A sliding window alone silently drops facts established early; pairing it with a structured state object for durable values plus selective retention of decisions keeps the transactional details addressable while bounding token growth. The rolling prose recap is the strong near-miss — it does preserve some history, but repeated re-summarisation blurs exactly the order IDs and amounts a support agent must quote precisely.

questions.q: Why is a structured state object preferable to a prose running summary for tracking a Claude agent's accumulated facts across compaction cycles?
options: It occupies far more tokens than equivalent prose, which devotes a much larger share of the window to the agent's accumulated facts
It keeps values addressable and unambiguous: fields are read, updated, and validated individually, while prose blurs specifics on re-summarisation
Prose summaries must be re-summarised on every compaction cycle, whereas structured state is carried forward untouched and never needs updating
Structured state can be validated against a schema, letting the runtime reject any compaction whose output has dropped a required field
questions.explain: Structured fields stay individually readable, updatable, and verifiable, so specific values survive repeated compaction, whereas each re-summarisation of prose loses precision. Schema validation of the state is the near-miss — it is a genuine side benefit, but the core reason is addressability of the values themselves, and validation alone would not stop prose from blurring.

questions.q: Your GitHub Actions workflow needs Claude Code to review each pull request on a runner with no TTY, and a later step must parse the result. Which invocation shape is correct?
options: Run `claude -p` with the review prompt plus `--verbose`, then scrape the streamed thinking blocks for the reviewer's final conclusions.
Run `claude` with the review prompt as a positional argument, then pipe the interactive transcript to a parsing step later in the job.
Run `claude -p` with the review prompt plus `--output-format json`, so the run is non-interactive and the result is machine-parseable.
Run `claude --continue` with the review prompt so the job reuses the previous run's session and prints its final result to standard out.
questions.explain: Print mode (`-p`/`--print`) is the non-interactive entry point, and `--output-format json` gives the later step a stable structure to parse. The near-miss is invoking `claude` with a positional prompt: without print mode Claude Code starts an interactive session, which a TTY-less runner cannot drive.

questions.q: A nightly Claude Code CI job occasionally loops on a flaky test, burning hours of runtime and API spend before the job timeout kills it. Which configuration most directly bounds both the work and the spend of the run?
options: Set `--max-turns` and `--max-budget-usd` on the print-mode invocation, so the run stops once either the turn cap or the dollar cap is hit.
Set `--max-turns` and lower the job's runner timeout, relying on the CI platform to stop the run before meaningful API spend accrues.
Set `--permission-mode plan` and `--verbose` so the run only proposes work, which keeps its cost inherently bounded on every invocation.
Set `--fallback-model` to a cheaper model and lower the reasoning effort, so each turn costs less even when the agent loops on a bad test.
questions.explain: `--max-turns` and `--max-budget-usd` are print-mode caps that stop the run on turns and on dollars respectively, and subagent spend counts toward the budget cap. The near-miss pairs the right turn cap with a runner timeout: wall-clock termination bounds job duration but not the spend already incurred, and it gives no graceful exit.

questions.q: Your CI job posts Claude's review findings as individual line comments. A shell script currently regex-scrapes the markdown Claude prints, and it breaks whenever the prose wording shifts. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Run print mode with `--json-schema` describing the finding objects, so the run emits validated JSON that the posting step consumes directly.
Have the job run the review twice and post only findings whose scraped text matches across both runs, discarding any that differ at all.
Add a strict system prompt fixing the markdown headings and bullet wording, then keep the existing regex scraper pointed at that format.
Pipe the printed markdown into a second print-mode Claude Code call that reformats it as JSON before the posting step reads the findings.
questions.explain: `--json-schema` in print mode makes the run emit output validated against the schema you supply, so the posting step parses fields instead of prose. The near-miss is pinning the markdown format via the system prompt: formatting instructions are best-effort, so the scraper stays one wording drift away from breaking again.

questions.q: Your review bot runs on every push to a pull request. On the third push it re-posts the same three comments about a deliberate custom error wrapper that the author already replied to and dismissed. What is the best fix?
options: Have the posting step compare new comment bodies against the pull request's existing comments and drop exact text matches before posting.
Narrow the review to only the files touched by the most recent push, so previously reviewed code cannot produce the same findings again.
Pass the prior run's findings and the project's accepted patterns in as review context, so the agent skips issues already raised or excluded.
Instruct the reviewer to be conservative and report only issues it is highly confident about, which will suppress the repeated comments.
questions.explain: Feeding prior findings and the codebase's accepted patterns into each run stops the agent re-deriving the same issue, and persistent convention context is what keeps a deliberate pattern from being flagged at all. The near-miss is text-matching comments before posting: it hides exact repeats but not reworded ones, and the agent still spends the run rediscovering them.

questions.q: A CI pipeline has Claude Code generate a feature implementation and then, in the same session, asks it to review its own diff. The review almost never finds problems. Which change best addresses this?
options: Extend the same session with a review turn instructing the agent to adopt a skeptical persona and re-read every file it has just written.
Run the review as a separate Claude Code instance that sees only the diff and the project standards, not the authoring session's reasoning.
Keep the single session but raise the turn limit, giving the agent room to iterate over its own output before it reports any findings.
Keep the single session but require a confidence score per file, and escalate only the files scoring below a fixed review threshold.
questions.explain: An independent instance reviews the diff without the authoring session's rationale in context, so it does not inherit the assumptions that produced the defect. The near-miss is a skeptical-persona turn in the same session: the flawed reasoning is still in context, so the model tends to re-justify its own work rather than challenge it.

questions.q: Claude Code generates unit tests in CI, but the output uses a mocking library the repo does not use, ignores the shared fixture factory, and mostly asserts that constructors return non-null values. How do you most improve this?
options: Raise the turn limit and request more tests per module, so broader coverage compensates for weak assertions in any individual test case.
Add a lint step that rejects any test importing an unapproved library, and re-run generation until the produced suite passes that check.
Supply representative existing test files and the fixture conventions as context, plus criteria separating behavioral tests from trivial ones.
Switch generation to plan mode so the agent proposes a test plan for approval before writing any assertions against the new modules.
questions.explain: Existing tests show the mocking library and fixture factory by example, and explicit criteria for a behavioral assertion stop the model settling for non-null checks. The near-miss is the lint gate: it can reject the wrong import but cannot teach fixture conventions or turn a trivial assertion into a meaningful one.

questions.q: Your team wants an internal analytics MCP server available to everyone who clones the repository, with the same command and arguments, and reviewed like any other change. Which configuration approach fits?
options: Add it at user scope in each developer's own configuration, and document the exact add command in the repository's contributor guide.
Add it at local scope in the repository checkout so it applies to that project directory only and travels with the cloned working tree.
Ship a setup task that runs the add command at session start, so the server is registered freshly for each developer on every machine.
Add it at project scope so the definition lands in the repository's checked-in `.mcp.json` and is reviewed and shared like any other change.
questions.explain: Project scope writes the server into `.mcp.json` at the repo root, which is committed, so every clone gets the same definition and changes go through code review. The near-miss is user scope plus documentation: it works per machine but drifts silently, since nothing keeps each developer's private configuration in step with the repo.

questions.q: The checked-in `.mcp.json` for that analytics server needs an API key. Keys differ per developer and must never be committed to the repository. What is the right configuration?
options: Store the key in the CI secret store and have a setup script rewrite `.mcp.json` with the literal value before each interactive session.
Commit a placeholder key value in `.mcp.json` and have each developer edit it locally, keeping that edited file out of every future commit.
Move the whole server definition to user scope for everyone, because a project-scoped configuration cannot carry any credential material.
Reference the key as `${ANALYTICS_API_KEY}` in the server's env block, so each developer supplies the value from their own environment.
questions.explain: Claude Code expands `${VAR}` references in `.mcp.json`, so the shared file stays secret-free while each developer's environment supplies the value. The near-miss is a committed placeholder edited locally: it puts real credentials in a tracked file, where a routine commit leaks them.

questions.q: After adding an MCP server, a developer reports that Claude 'does not know about' its tools. You need to establish whether Claude Code actually connected to the server. What do you check first?
options: Ask Claude inside the session to list the tools it can call, and treat the absence of that server's tools as proof the config is invalid.
Re-add the server at a broader scope, since tool discovery only happens for servers configured at user scope rather than project scope.
Inspect the server process logs for inbound traffic, since a connected client always writes a discovery request the server records in a log.
Check the server's connection status in the MCP server listing, since a server that fails to connect or awaits approval exposes no tools.
questions.explain: Listing the MCP servers shows a per-server status such as connected, needs authentication, or failed to connect, which separates a config problem from a connection or approval problem. The near-miss is asking Claude what tools it has: the symptom is confirmed but the cause is not, and a model's self-report of its tool list is not a diagnostic.

questions.q: A support MCP server exposes a `search_docs` tool. Agents spend many turns calling it repeatedly to page through a small, stable refund policy handbook before they can answer. What is the better design?
options: Keep the tool but widen its result limit so one call returns the whole handbook, and instruct agents to call it exactly once per case.
Keep the tool and add a `get_policy_section` tool, so agents can jump straight to a named section instead of paging through search hits.
Expose the handbook documents as MCP resources the client can attach directly, so agents read them without exploratory search tool calls.
Drop the tool and inline the handbook text into the agent's system prompt at the start of every support case the agent picks up.
questions.explain: Resources are addressable content the client can fetch and attach, which is the right fit for a small stable corpus and removes the exploratory search loop entirely. The near-miss is adding `get_policy_section`: it shortens the loop but still spends a model turn and a tool call to retrieve content that could simply be attached.

questions.q: An extraction service must always return a record through your `record_invoice` tool, but the model sometimes answers in prose, and sometimes calls `record_invoice` before calling `fetch_vendor` for the vendor ID it needs. How do you fix both?
options: Force `record_invoice` with `tool_choice`, and mark the vendor ID required so the model must fetch it before it can populate the record.
Set `tool_choice` to `any` for the exchange, so the model must call some tool each turn and will therefore order the two calls correctly.
Leave `tool_choice` on auto, add a prompt line requiring the lookup first, and retry the request whenever the reply comes back as prose.
Force `record_invoice` with `tool_choice`, and sequence the work so the vendor lookup happens in an earlier call whose result is passed in.
questions.explain: Forcing the specific tool guarantees the structured call instead of prose, and because the forced turn cannot also call `fetch_vendor`, the prerequisite lookup has to be its own earlier step whose result is fed forward. The near-miss relies on a required schema field to force the lookup: a required field only makes the model fill the slot, which it can do by guessing rather than by calling `fetch_vendor`.

questions.q: A long Claude Code session has mapped a 2,000-file service. Overnight another team merged changes to eight of those files. You resume the session the next morning. How do you most efficiently restore correctness?
options: Ask the agent to redo its original exploration from scratch, since any cached understanding of the service may now be silently outdated.
Resume the session and name the eight changed files, so the agent re-reads only those and updates the understanding it already holds.
Resume the session and ask the agent to diff its own notes against the repository, letting it decide for itself which files to re-read.
Start a new session with the merge diff attached, discarding the earlier mapping because a resumed session's context cannot be corrected.
questions.explain: Resumption preserves the expensive mapping, and injecting the list of changed files scopes re-analysis to exactly the stale portion. The near-miss is having the agent diff its own notes against the repo: it is targeted in spirit but spends many turns rediscovering what the merge already told you precisely.

questions.q: A three-hour debugging session is near its context limit, and most of the history is verbose tool output describing a database schema that has since been redesigned. You must continue the work tomorrow. Which approach is best?
options: Start a fresh session and inject a written summary of the conclusions and the new schema, leaving the obsolete tool output behind entirely.
Resume the session with forking so the original transcript is preserved, then carry on from the same accumulated tool results as before.
Resume the session and prepend a note that the schema changed, relying on the agent to prefer that note over the stale output it holds.
Resume the session and compact the history, trusting compaction to drop the obsolete schema output while retaining the useful conclusions.
questions.explain: When most of the accumulated context is actively wrong, a fresh session seeded with a curated summary is both cheaper and safer than carrying contradictory material forward. The near-miss is resuming and compacting: compaction shrinks the transcript but you do not control what it keeps, so the outdated schema can survive into the summary and keep misleading the agent.

questions.q: A nightly pipeline runs a coordinator over 400 repositories with analysis subagents. When the runner is preempted at repository 300, the entire run restarts from zero the next night. Which design change fixes this?
options: Raise each subagent's turn limit and run repositories in larger parallel batches, so the pipeline finishes before preemption can occur.
Persist per-repository status and results to durable external state as each finishes, so a restart resumes at the first unprocessed repo.
Have each subagent retry its own repository on failure, so an interrupted worker recovers locally and the coordinator never has to restart.
Have the coordinator hold every per-repository result in its own context and emit them at the end, so a restart can reuse that state.
questions.explain: Externalising per-unit progress as work completes makes the pipeline resumable: a restart reads the manifest and skips everything already done. The near-miss keeps results in the coordinator's context, which dies with the process and also grows the context window until quality degrades.

questions.q: An invoice extraction pipeline sends 10% of documents to human reviewers, chosen at random. Reviewers mostly confirm easy documents while real errors keep reaching downstream systems. How should routing be redesigned?
options: Route on the overall document confidence score alone, sending every document scoring below one tuned global threshold to a human reviewer.
Route on field-level confidence and document characteristics, so ambiguous fields and unusual document types reach a reviewer every time.
Raise the random sample to 30% of documents, since a larger uniform sample will catch proportionally more of the errors going downstream.
Route the documents that needed the most extraction retries, since retry count is the clearest signal available that a document was hard.
questions.explain: Targeting review at low-confidence fields and at document characteristics known to be difficult puts human attention where the errors actually are, instead of spending it on easy documents. The near-miss is a single document-level confidence threshold: it is confidence-driven but a document with one badly ambiguous field can still score high overall and bypass review.

questions.q: Your extraction pipeline reports 96% field accuracy overall and the team proposes cutting human review. One vendor's handwritten remittance advices make up 4% of volume. What is the key risk in that number?
options: Accuracy is measured against reviewer-corrected data, so the figure is circular and cannot support any decision about review volume at all.
Accuracy without a confidence interval is unusable, so the number must be recomputed with error bars before any decision is defensible.
An aggregate can hide a document type that performs far worse; a rare handwritten class could fail badly and barely move the overall figure.
Field accuracy weights every field equally, so the number says nothing about whether throughput can absorb a reduction in human review.
questions.explain: A volume-weighted aggregate is dominated by the easy majority, so a 4% class could be near-random and still leave the headline near 96%. The near-miss is the circularity objection: reviewer-corrected ground truth is a real methodological caveat, but it does not explain why a small hard class is invisible in the aggregate.

questions.q: Before reducing human review on your extraction pipeline, the team wants evidence that doing so is safe. Which validation gives the strongest basis for deciding where review can be cut?
options: One held-out sample drawn uniformly from recent volume and scored overall, with review reduced once the total error rate looks acceptable.
A production test that halves review for one traffic group and compares downstream correction tickets between groups over a full quarter.
A calibration check that reported confidence scores match observed accuracy, with review reduced wherever reported confidence is high.
Accuracy measured per document type and per field against ground truth, with review retained for the type-and-field pairs that fall short.
questions.explain: Segmenting accuracy by document type and field shows exactly which slices are safe to automate and which must stay under review, rather than trading a blanket decision on one number. The near-miss is the calibration check: well-calibrated confidence is necessary but not sufficient, because a type can be confidently and consistently wrong.

questions.q: A review call asks Claude to return a JSON array of findings for a 4,000-line diff. The response is consistently cut off mid-object and fails schema validation, even though the schema itself is correct. What is the right fix?
options: Split the diff into smaller scoped review calls that each return a valid findings array, and merge the results once all the calls finish.
Raise the output token limit to the model's ceiling so the whole findings array fits, and validate that single response against the schema.
Relax the schema so partial objects still validate, then repair the truncated final entry in post-processing before the findings are merged.
Retry the same call with the validation error fed back, so the model emits a shorter array that fits within the available response budget.
questions.explain: Truncation is an output-length problem, and scoping each call to a slice of the diff keeps every response comfortably inside the limit while the merge reconstructs the full finding set. The near-miss is raising the token ceiling: it may buy headroom for this diff but the failure returns on the next larger one, and it does nothing about quality loss over a very long single response.
